title: Forcing Your Wife to Take Her Words Seriously
author: M.A. Franklin
summary: M.A. Franklin builds a piece on household authority out of one enforced consequence. His eleven-year-old daughter was told she would lose a week of summer camp if caught lying again, was caught within the week, and lost the camp, over his wife's objection that the punishment fell harder on the parents than on the child. Franklin's claim is that following through taught the whole household, including the younger brothers who watched the drop-off not happen, and that the family has had one lying incident since. The theological argument is the essay's spine. He reads Numbers 30 as making a husband responsible for his wife's vows by his silence: if he does not oppose the thoughtless utterance on the day he hears it, he establishes it, and its breach becomes his own. From this he draws a striking reframe of the husband's role, that upholding or nullifying a spouse's word is a protection offered to her rather than a check on her, sparing her either a foolish word or the worse fate of not keeping her word. The piece ends by deliberately separating consequence from coldness, describing a week of intentional fun designed to signal the daughter was not a burden.
points: The load-bearing move is that the father's silence when the threat was made converted his wife's off-the-cuff vow into his own binding promise.
Franklin reads the pedagogy as ambient rather than targeted, since the siblings who watched the consequence land learned the lesson without receiving it.
Numbers 30 is used to argue a husband forfeits the excuse that his wife was the one who said it, and cannot seethe quietly and hope the matter dissolves.
The essay frames confrontation as unavoidable and merely schedulable, either now over the foolish word or later over the broken one.
The closing week of family outings is presented as the necessary counterweight, making clear the punishment was about the daughter's soul rather than her burdensomeness.
quotes: We don’t have a problem with lying in my house. At least, not anymore. My children confess fairly quickly if they do something wrong and are asked directly about it, and they rarely try to hide something.
It was a lesson not only for our daughter, but also for her younger brothers. They knew why their sister was not able to go. They knew why she wasn’t dropped off.
If I had let my wife talk me out of keeping our promise, the boys (and certainly their older sister) would have learned a far different lesson. One that would have undermined our entire household.

It would have been so easy to cave. To give our daughter another chance and another empty threat, and she would have lied again and again until we finally did something equally drastic. Worse, all of my children would have taken my wife’s words far less seriously.

But notice how I said our promise above. It was my wife who made the threat. At the time, in the back of my mind, I thought about countermanding her order, because I knew it was off-the-cuff and given in anger. I thought better of it.

And from that moment on, it became my promise, too. My silence was an endorsement. As the head of the household, keeping that promise now became my responsibility. If we failed to carry it out, it would be more my failure than my wife’s.

What goes on in the house, what is spoken, is the responsibility of the husband. He does not get to make the excuse, “But my wife was the one who said that!” He established her word by remaining silent, by not confronting her.

This protection is a valuable gift a husband can provide for his wife. Either he can protect her from a foolish word, or he can prevent her from doing an equally foolish thing: not keeping her word. Confrontation now, or possible confrontation later?
